title: CCTP bridging charges two rate limits at once, an aggregate and a per-destination one, and refuses a zero mint recipient
content:
A.6.1.1.3.2.6.1.2.2.1.1.2.1.2.6.1.1 lists the checks in order: the contract "will trigger a rate limit decrease for the CCTP limit ID and amount," then "trigger a rate limit decrease for a domain-specific key and amount," then "require that `mintRecipient` is not zero, reverting if it is," then split the amount against Circle's "burn limit per message" into as many transfers as needed.

The double decrement implements a two-tier risk budget, matching the two limits recorded earlier in the Artifact: `LIMIT_USDC_TO_CCTP` bounds everything Keel bridges out of Ethereum in aggregate, while `LIMIT_USDC_TO_DOMAIN` bounds what may go to a single destination such as Solana. Neither alone would do the job — an aggregate-only limit would allow the whole budget to concentrate on the riskiest chain, and per-domain-only limits would sum to an unbounded total as domains are added.

The zero-address guard is a small but pointed check. Since the mint recipient is admin-configured per domain, a zero value means the domain was never configured; without the guard, a bridge into an unconfigured domain would burn USDC on Ethereum and mint it to nobody. The revert converts a silent, irreversible loss into a failed transaction.

Splitting against the per-message burn limit is a third-party constraint, not a Sky one — the same pattern as the PSM fill loop. Keel's operational logic is substantially shaped by the transaction-level ceilings of the external protocols it rides on.
description: transferUSDCToCCTP decrements both the global CCTP limit and a domain-specific key, requires a non-zero mintRecipient, and splits transfers exceeding Circle's per-message burn limit.
